chapters.title: Building a sentence in English
chapters.subtitle: Word order, the present tenses and the questions you need every day at work.

body.p: Spanish lets you move words around freely: «Trabaja Luis aquí», «Luis trabaja aquí», «Aquí trabaja Luis» — all correct. English does not. English carries meaning in the order of the words, so the order is almost fixed. This single fact explains most beginner mistakes.

body.key: The basic order is SUBJECT → VERB → OBJECT, and you cannot drop the subject. In Spanish «Trabajo aquí» is complete; in English you must say I work here.

body.p: Use it for what is generally true or what you do regularly: I work at a workshop. The engine uses diesel. He starts at six.

body.code:
I / you / we / they  →  work
he / she / it        →  works   ← the -s that everyone forgets

body.p: That final -s in the third person is the most common mistake for Spanish speakers, because Spanish marks the person in the verb ending and English almost never does. English only has this one ending, so it feels unimportant — but a missing -s is heard immediately.

body.h: Questions and negatives need a helper

body.p: This is the second big difference. In Spanish you make a question with intonation. In English you need the auxiliary do or does, and when it appears, the main verb goes back to its base form:

body.code:
Statement:  He works on Saturdays.
Question:   Does he work on Saturdays?      (not: does he works)
Negative:   He doesn't work on Saturdays.   (not: he doesn't works)

body.note: Short answers keep the auxiliary, not the verb: Do you work here? — Yes, I do. Answering just «yes» sounds abrupt, and repeating the whole verb sounds foreign.

body.p: Formed with am / is / are + verb-ing, it describes what is going on at this moment or around this period: I am checking the oil right now. We are working on the north site this month.

Compare the two tenses in a work context. I repair engines is your job. I am repairing an engine is what you are doing while you speak. Spanish uses the simple present for both, which is why the continuous feels optional — it is not.

body.warn: Some verbs describe states, not actions, and they do not take the continuous: know, need, want, believe, understand, belong, cost. Say I need a wrench, never I am needing a wrench.

body.p: The Past Simple has one form for every person, which makes it easier than Spanish. Regular verbs add -ed; irregular verbs have to be learned one by one.

body.code:
Regular:    work → worked      check → checked
Irregular:  go → went         take → took
            buy → bought       break → broke

Negative / question use DID + base form:
  I didn't go.      Did you see it?   (not: did you saw)

body.p: Notice the same pattern as the present: once the auxiliary did appears, the main verb loses its past form. English marks the tense only once, in the auxiliary.

list: going to — a plan already decided, or clear evidence: I'm going to change the oil tomorrow. / Look at that smoke — it's going to break down.
will — a decision made while speaking, an offer, a prediction: I'll help you with that. / It will probably rain.
Present Continuous — a fixed arrangement with a time and place: I'm meeting the supplier at four.

body.p: English divides nouns into things you can count and things you cannot, and this changes the words around them.

body.code:
COUNTABLE      a bolt, two bolts     How many bolts?    a few bolts
UNCOUNTABLE    oil, fuel, work       How much oil?      a little oil

body.p: Watch out for words that are countable in Spanish but not in English: information, advice, equipment, work, money, news. You cannot say an information or two advices; you say a piece of information, some advice.

body.code:
TIME      at 7 o'clock   ·   on Monday   ·   in June / in 2026
PLACE     at the workshop ·  on the table ·  in the truck

Rule of thumb: at = a point, on = a surface or day, in = inside a space or period

body.p: Spanish has un/una/el/la and uses them almost everywhere. English uses them less, and the choice follows a different logic: a/an introduces something for the first time or says what kind of thing it is; the points at something both people already know about.

body.code:
I need A wrench.          (any wrench — first mention)
Pass me THE wrench.       (the one we both can see)
He is A mechanic.         (job → always a/an in English)
THE engine is hot.        (the one we're working on)

body.p: Choose a or an by the sound, not the letter: an hour (the h is silent), a university (it sounds «yu»), an SUV (it sounds «es»).

body.warn: English uses no article for general statements in plural or with uncountables: Diesel engines last longer, not The diesel engines last longer. Spanish speakers add the here constantly — it is one of the easiest mistakes to hear.

body.code:
REGULAR      bolt → bolts      hose → hoses
-Y → -IES    company → companies
-F → -VES    knife → knives     leaf → leaves
IRREGULAR    man → men          woman → women
             child → children   foot → feet
             tooth → teeth      person → people

body.p: For possession English does not say «the door of the truck» — it prefers 's with people and living things, and often just puts two nouns together for objects:

body.code:
the mechanic'S tools       (person → 's)
the truck door             (two nouns together)
the engine'S power    o    the power OF the engine   (both work)

body.note: Two nouns together is extremely common in technical English, and the last word is the real thing: oil filter is a filter, filter oil would be oil. Brake fluid, fuel pump, safety helmet, service manual.

body.code:
There IS a leak.               singular
There IS some oil on the floor. uncountable
There ARE two trucks outside.  plural

There ISN'T any fuel left.
ARE there any spare filters?

body.p: Use some in positive sentences and any in negatives and questions: There's some oil / There isn't any oil / Is there any oil?

body.h: Can and can't: ability, permission, requests

body.code:
I CAN drive a forklift.        ability
You CAN'T park here.           prohibition
CAN you help me?               request
CAN I use this tool?           permission

body.p: can never takes to and never changes: he cans, can to drive are both wrong. Its past is could. And listen to the difference: can is short and weak in speech, while can't is longer and stressed — that is how native speakers tell them apart.

body.code:
WHAT      What is that noise?
WHERE     Where is the manual?
WHEN      When did it start?
WHO       Who repaired it?
WHY       Why is it overheating?
HOW       How does it work?
WHICH     Which one is broken?     (a choice between few)
HOW LONG  How long have you worked here?
HOW OFTEN How often do you service it?

body.p: The word order after the question word is the same as any question: question word + auxiliary + subject + verb. Where did you put it?, not Where you put it?
The imperative is just the base verb with no subject. It is what manuals, signs and colleagues use all day:

body.code:
Check the oil level.
Don't start the engine.
Always wear a helmet.
Never open the radiator when it's hot.
Please hold this.

body.note: The imperative is neutral, not rude, in written instructions. But when asking a person for something, soften it: Could you check the oil? sounds much better than Check the oil.

body.h: Adjectives: two rules and you're done

list: They go before the noun: a hydraulic pump, not a pump hydraulic.
They never take a plural -s: two big trucks, not two bigs trucks.

body.p: When you stack several, the order sounds natural to natives and strange to learners: opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose. A nice big old yellow Japanese hydraulic pump. Don't memorise the list — just avoid stacking more than two or three.

body.h: The irregular verbs you cannot avoid

body.code:
BASE      PAST       PARTICIPLE
be        was/were   been
go        went       gone
do        did        done
have      had        had
make      made       made
take      took       taken
get       got        got/gotten
come      came       come
see       saw        seen
buy       bought     bought
bring     brought    brought
break     broke      broken
drive     drove      driven
put       put        put
read      read       read      (spelling same, sound changes)

body.key: Learn them in the three-column form from day one. The third column is useless today, but it is exactly what you will need for the Present Perfect and the passive at B1 — and relearning them later costs twice as much.

body.code:
13 thirteen  /  30 thirty     ← listen for the stress
1,500  one thousand five hundred  (comma = thousands)
3.5    three point five           (point = decimal)

7:15  quarter past seven   ·  7:45  quarter to eight
7:30  half past seven      ·  7:05  five past seven

UK: 29 August 2026  ·  US: August 29, 2026

body.warn: Dates in numbers are dangerous: 03/08/2026 is 3 August in the UK and 8 March in the US. In any document that matters, write the month in letters.

list: get up — leave your bed: I get up at five.
turn on / turn off — a machine or a light: Turn off the engine.
put on / take off — clothes and equipment: Put on your gloves.
pick up / drop off — collect or leave something: I'll pick up the parts.
fill up — fill completely: Fill up the tank.
look for — search: I'm looking for a 14 mm wrench.
come back / go back — return: I'll come back tomorrow.
write down — note: Write down the code.

body.note: Remember the pronoun rule from the start: Turn it off ✅, never turn off it. It costs nothing to learn now and saves a habit later.

body.h: Two sounds that change the meaning

body.p: English marks grammar with endings that are easy to swallow, and swallowing them makes you hard to understand:

list: The -s of the third person and of plurals: he works, two bolts. Pronounced /s/ after a voiceless sound, /z/ after a voiced one, and /ɪz/ after s, sh, ch, x: hoses, watches.
The -ed of the past: /t/ after voiceless (checked), /d/ after voiced (repaired), and /ɪd/ only after t or d (wanted, needed).

body.p: Notice that worked is one syllable, not two. Saying «work-ed» is the single most recognisable Spanish-speaker mistake, and it is easy to fix once you hear it.

body.h: to be or to have: the trap Spanish sets for you

body.p: Spanish uses tener for age, hunger, cold and being right. English uses to be for all of them, and the mistake is instantly recognisable.

body.code:
I AM 34 (years old).       not: I have 34
I AM hungry / thirsty.      not: I have hunger
I AM cold / hot.            not: I have cold
I AM right / wrong.         not: I have reason
I AM afraid.                not: I have fear
I AM in a hurry.            not: I have hurry

BUT with to have:
I HAVE a headache.   I HAVE a problem.   I HAVE time.

body.note: There is one more: How old are you? — never how many years do you have. If you fix only one thing from this section, fix this question, because you will be asked it constantly.

body.p: Spanish drops the subject freely; English never can. And when there is no real subject, English invents one — the word it, which means nothing at all here.

body.code:
IT is raining.              (Llueve)
IT is cold today.           (Hace frío hoy)
IT is seven o'clock.        (Son las siete)
IT is important to check.   (Es importante revisar)
IT takes two hours.         (Toma dos horas)

THERE is a problem.         (Hay un problema)
THERE are two trucks.       (Hay dos camiones)

body.warn: Don't confuse the two empty subjects. There is/are says that something exists; it is describes a situation. There is a problem ✅ / It has a problem ❌ when you mean «hay un problema».

body.h: Pronouns: the small words that carry everything

body.code:
SUBJECT   OBJECT    POSSESSIVE adj   POSSESSIVE pron
I         me        my               mine
you       you       your             yours
he        him       his              his
she       her       her              hers
it        it        its              its
we        us        our              ours
they      them      their            theirs

HE gave the manual to ME.  →  It's HIS manual, not MINE.

body.p: Two things to watch. First, its (possessive) has no apostrophe, while it's means it is — even native speakers get this wrong. Second, the possessive matches the owner, not the object: Ana and her truck, Luis and his tools. Spanish uses su for both, so this needs conscious practice.

body.h: Verbs followed by -ing: like, love, hate

body.code:
I LIKE working outdoors.
I LOVE fixing engines.
I DON'T MIND working weekends.
I HATE waiting.
I ENJOY learning new things.

I'D LIKE TO learn English.    ← 'would like' takes TO

body.p: Note the difference: I like = in general, always. I'd like (I would like) = I want, right now. I like coffee is a preference; I'd like a coffee is an order at the counter.

body.code:
PLACE (static)
  IN the truck · IN the box · IN Managua
  ON the table · ON the wall · ON the floor
  AT the workshop · AT home · AT work
  UNDER · BEHIND · IN FRONT OF · NEXT TO · BETWEEN

MOVEMENT
  go TO the workshop      (destination)
  come FROM the office    (origin)
  put it INTO the box     (entering)
  get ON / OFF the truck  (a large vehicle)
  get IN / OUT OF the car (a small one)

body.warn: Go to always takes to — except with home: I go home, never I go to home. And arrive takes at or in, never to: I arrived at the workshop.

body.h: Spelling when you add an ending

body.code:
-ING
  make → making        (drop the silent -e)
  stop → stopping      (double the final consonant)
  run  → running

-ED
  use  → used
  stop → stopped
  try  → tried         (-y after consonant → -ied)
  play → played        (-y after vowel → just -ed)

-S
  work → works
  watch → watches      (add -es after s, sh, ch, x)
  study → studies
  go → goes

body.p: The doubling rule has a logic: it keeps the vowel short. Hoping and hopping are different words, and the double letter is what tells you which one you're reading.

body.h: Words that look Spanish but aren't

body.code:
actually      = in fact         (actualmente = currently)
assist        = help            (asistir a = attend)
realize       = notice          (realizar = carry out)
support       = hold up, bear   (soportar = tolerate)
constipated   = estreñido       (constipado = has a cold)
embarrassed   = avergonzado     (embarazada = pregnant)
carpet        = alfombra        (carpeta = folder)
exit          = salida          (éxito = success)

body.note: The last three cause real trouble. Say I'm embarrassed only if you mean ashamed — and if you have a cold, the word is simply I have a cold.

body.quote: I work at a workshop in Managua. Right now I'm repairing a hydraulic pump. Yesterday I checked the oil and I found a leak, so I'm going to replace the seal tomorrow. How much oil do we have left?

body.p: Six sentences, six structures: present simple, present continuous, past simple, going to, an uncountable question. If you can produce this paragraph about your own day, you have A2 under control.

body.key: Do not study these tenses as a list to memorise. Take one real situation from your work each day and describe it out loud in three sentences: what you do generally, what you are doing now, what you did yesterday.

chapters.title: Getting things done in English
chapters.subtitle: The words and phrases you need to greet people, describe a problem, ask for what you need and survive a conversation you don't fully understand.

body.p: The first chapter gave you the machinery of the language. This one gives you the phrases: the things you actually say at work, in a shop, on the phone. Most of them you can learn as whole blocks, without analysing the grammar — and that is exactly how children and good adult learners do it.

body.code:
Good morning / afternoon / evening.
Hi. / Hello. / Morning!            (informal, very common)
How are you? — Fine, thanks. And you?
How's it going? — Not bad, thanks.
Nice to meet you. — Nice to meet you too.

See you tomorrow. / See you later. / Take care.
Have a good weekend. — You too!

body.p: Good night is only for saying goodbye at the end of the day, never for greeting someone. To greet someone in the evening you say good evening.

body.note: «How are you?» is often a greeting, not a real question. The expected answer is short — Fine, thanks — and then you return it. Giving a long honest answer surprises people.

body.quote: Hi, I'm Luis. I'm a heavy machinery mechanic. I work for a construction company in Managua. I've been doing this for about ten years. I'm learning English because I want to read the technical manuals.

body.p: Learn your own version of this paragraph by heart. It is the single most useful thing you can memorise, because you will need it every time you meet someone new, and reciting it fluently buys you confidence for the rest of the conversation.

body.code:
I'm from Nicaragua.
I live in Managua.
I work FOR a company.       (employer)
I work AT a workshop.        (place)
I work AS a mechanic.        (role)
I'm responsible FOR maintenance.

body.p: The grammar is easy; the politeness is what matters. English sounds rude very quickly without these softeners.

body.code:
DIRECT (can sound rude)     POLITE
Give me the wrench.      →  COULD you pass me the wrench, please?
I want a coffee.         →  I'D LIKE a coffee, please.
Help me.                 →  COULD you give me a hand?
Repeat that.             →  SORRY, could you repeat that?
Where is the office?     →  EXCUSE ME, where is the office?

body.key: Three words do almost all the work: please, sorry and excuse me. Use excuse me to get someone's attention or to pass by, and sorry to apologise or when you didn't hear.

body.p: This is the most valuable section of the chapter. Pretending to understand is what really breaks a conversation — asking never does.

body.code:
Sorry, I didn't catch that.
Could you repeat that, please?
Could you speak more slowly, please?
Could you write it down?
How do you spell that?
What does «gasket» mean?
How do you say «empaque» in English?
Sorry, my English isn't very good.
Just to make sure — you mean the front one?

body.note: «I didn't catch that» is what native speakers say, and it sounds much better than «I don't understand», because it puts the problem on the noise, not on you.

body.p: A whole conversation at work can be built from a handful of patterns:

body.code:
There is a problem WITH the pump.
The engine DOESN'T start.
It's NOT working.
It STOPPED working yesterday.
It makes a strange noise.
There's a leak / a crack / a loose bolt.
The oil is dirty.
It's overheating.
I think the filter is blocked.
It needs a new seal.

list: broken — roto, no funciona
loose ↔ tight — flojo ↔ apretado
worn out — gastado
leaking — con fuga · dripping — goteando
stuck — atascado, pegado
missing — falta, no está
noisy — ruidoso · smooth — suave

body.code:
TOOLS        wrench/spanner · screwdriver · hammer · pliers
             socket · tape measure · jack · grinder · drill
FASTENERS    bolt · nut · washer · screw · clamp · pin
PARTS        bearing · gasket · seal · hose · belt · filter
             valve · pump · piston · spring · gear
MATERIALS    steel · rubber · copper · plastic · grease · oil
CONDITION    new · used · second-hand · spare · faulty

body.p: Two spelling notes: pliers and scissors are always plural (a pair of pliers), and equipment never takes an -s (a lot of equipment, not equipments).

body.h: Numbers you have to hear correctly

body.code:
13 THIRteen  ·  30 THIRty      the stress moves!
14 fourTEEN  ·  40 FORty
15 fifTEEN   ·  50 FIFty

0   zero (US) · oh (in phone numbers) · nil (sports)
1/2 a half   ·  1/4 a quarter  ·  3/4 three quarters
1.5 one point five
1,500 one thousand five hundred / fifteen hundred

14 mm  fourteen millimetres
3/8"   three eighths of an inch

body.warn: The -teen / -ty pair is the number one source of expensive mistakes at work: ordering 50 filters instead of 15. When it matters, confirm: «One five, fifteen?» Native speakers do this too.

body.code:
MONDAY Tuesday Wednesday Thursday Friday Saturday Sunday
January February March April May June July
August September October November December

What time is it? — It's half past two.
What time do you start? — At seven.
How long does it take? — About three hours.
When is it ready? — On Friday. / In two days. / Next week.

yesterday · today · tomorrow · the day after tomorrow
last week · this week · next week
every day · twice a week · once a month

body.note: Days and months are always capitalised in English: Monday, August. Spanish writes them lowercase, so this is an easy point to lose in writing.

body.code:
Hello, this is Luis (speaking).
Can I speak to Mr. Ramírez, please?
Who's calling? — It's Luis, from the workshop.
Hold on a moment, please.
He's not available right now.
Can I leave a message?
Can you call me back?
Sorry, the line is bad. Could you repeat that?
Thanks for your time. Goodbye.

body.p: On the phone English says this is Luis, not I am Luis. It is a fixed expression — don't try to make it logical, just use it.

body.code:
I'm looking for a fuel filter for a CAT 320.
Do you have it in stock?
How much is it? / How much does it cost?
How much are they?         (plural)
Can you order it for me?
How long will it take?
Is there a cheaper option?
Can I have a receipt, please?
I'd like to pay by card / in cash.

AGREEING       Sure. · Of course. · No problem. · Absolutely.
               That's right. · Exactly. · I agree.
DECLINING      Sorry, I can't. · I'm afraid not.
               Not right now. · Maybe later.
NOT SURE       I'm not sure. · I think so. · I don't think so.
               Let me check. · I'll find out.

body.key: I'm afraid not and Let me check are worth more than a hundred vocabulary words. The first says no politely; the second buys you time without pretending you know.

body.p: English almost never answers with a bare yes or no. It repeats the auxiliary, and this is what makes a conversation sound natural:

body.code:
Do you work here?      — Yes, I DO.   / No, I DON'T.
Are you the mechanic?  — Yes, I AM.   / No, I'M NOT.
Can you fix it?        — Yes, I CAN.  / No, I CAN'T.
Have you finished?     — Yes, I HAVE. / No, I HAVEN'T.
Did you check it?      — Yes, I DID.  / No, I DIDN'T.

body.p: The rule is mechanical: whatever auxiliary appears in the question comes back in the answer. Practise it out loud until it is automatic — it costs one afternoon and changes how you sound.

body.code:
WRITTEN FULL       SPOKEN
I am               I'm
you are            you're
he is / he has     he's
we will            we'll
I would / I had    I'd
do not             don't
cannot             can't
is not             isn't
will not           won't

body.p: Native speakers use contractions almost always in speech and in informal writing. Not using them doesn't make you sound formal — it makes you sound like a textbook. Use them when you talk; write them out in a formal letter.

body.warn: Listen for won't (will not) and want — they are different words and beginners mix them constantly. And can't is longer and more stressed than can; that length is the only clue you'll get in fast speech.

body.p: If you remember nothing else from this chapter, remember these ten lines. They will get you through almost any situation:

list: Sorry, could you repeat that?
Could you speak more slowly, please?
How do you say … in English?
What does … mean?
Could you write it down?
Let me check and get back to you.
I'm not sure — I'll find out.
Could you give me a hand?
Just to make sure — you mean …?
Sorry, my English isn't very good, but I'm learning.

body.key: The last one changes every conversation. People are almost always patient with someone who is clearly trying — but they can't know you're trying unless you tell them.

chapters.title: Present Perfect and the logic of phrasal verbs
chapters.subtitle: The tense Spanish speakers get wrong, and how to stop memorising phrasal verbs one by one.

body.p: Two things separate a B1 speaker from an A2 one: using the Present Perfect correctly, and handling phrasal verbs without panic. Both look chaotic at first and both follow a clear logic.

body.h: Present Perfect: the bridge between past and present

body.p: Formed with have / has + past participle. The Spanish «he trabajado» looks identical, which is exactly the trap: the two languages use it at different moments.

body.code:
PAST SIMPLE       finished action, definite time
                  I repaired the pump YESTERDAY.

PRESENT PERFECT   no definite time, or still relevant now
                  I HAVE repaired three pumps this week.

body.key: The test is simple: if you say when, use the Past Simple. Words like yesterday, last week, in 2019, two hours ago force the Past Simple. Words like ever, never, already, yet, just, so far, this week point to the Present Perfect.

body.p: There is a second use that Spanish handles differently: an action that started in the past and continues now. Spanish uses the present («Trabajo aquí desde hace diez años»); English must use the perfect:

body.code:
I have worked here for ten years.        ✅
I have been working here for ten years.  ✅ (emphasis on the activity)
I work here since ten years.             ❌ never

list: for + a length of time: for ten years, for two hours, for a long time
since + the starting point: since 2016, since Monday, since I arrived

body.p: Present Perfect Simple looks at the result: I've repaired three engines today — three, done, countable. Present Perfect Continuous looks at the activity and its duration: I've been repairing engines all morning — that is why I am covered in oil.

body.note: A useful clue: if you can count the results, use the simple. If you are explaining why the present situation looks the way it does, use the continuous.

body.p: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle, and together they mean something new: break means romper, but break down means averiarse. English speakers use them constantly — avoiding them is what makes speech sound stiff and translated.
The good news: the particles carry consistent ideas. Once you feel them, you can often guess the meaning.

list: up — completing, increasing, finishing off: fill up, use up, eat up, speed up
down — reducing, stopping, writing: slow down, shut down, break down, write down
out — removing, discovering, exhausting: find out, run out, sort out, throw out
on — continuing, connecting: carry on, turn on, hold on, go on
off — separating, cancelling, disconnecting: turn off, call off, take off, put off
up with — enduring or producing: put up with, come up with, catch up with

body.p: This is the mechanical part, and it has one rule you must never break.

body.code:
SEPARABLE (verb + adverb)
  Turn off the engine.      ✅
  Turn the engine off.      ✅
  Turn it off.              ✅
  Turn off it.              ❌  ← pronoun MUST go in the middle

INSEPARABLE (verb + preposition)
  Look after the machine.   ✅
  Look after it.            ✅
  Look it after.            ❌

body.key: If you use a pronoun (it, them, him), a separable phrasal verb must be split. This single rule fixes more mistakes than memorising a hundred definitions.

body.h: The ones you will actually use at work

list: break down — stop working: The truck broke down on the road.
run out of — have no more left: We ran out of hydraulic oil.
find out — discover: I found out the filter was blocked.
figure out — understand after thinking: I can't figure out what's wrong.
look for — search: I'm looking for a 14 mm wrench.
look after — take care of: He looks after the machines.
carry out — perform a task: We carried out a full inspection.
put off — postpone: Don't put off the service.
give up — quit: Don't give up.
get on with — have a good relationship: I get on well with my boss.

body.p: In look forward to, be used to and get used to, the word to is a preposition, not part of an infinitive. What follows must be a noun or an -ing form:

body.code:
I look forward to hearing from you.   ✅
I look forward to hear from you.      ❌

I'm used to working long hours.       ✅ (I'm accustomed to it)
I used to work long hours.            ✅ (but not any more) — different verb!

body.warn: be used to and used to look almost identical and mean completely different things. I am used to the noise = I'm accustomed to it. I used to work at night = I did before, not now.

body.code:
MUST       obligation the speaker feels
           I must finish this today.
HAVE TO    obligation from outside (a rule)
           You have to wear a helmet on site.
SHOULD     advice, recommendation
           You should check the oil first.

body.warn: The negatives are opposites, and confusing them is dangerous: mustn't = it is forbidden (You mustn't smoke near the fuel tank). Don't have to = it isn't necessary (You don't have to stay late).

body.p: For the past, must borrows from have to: I had to replace it. And for regret, should have + participle: I should have checked the oil.
Formed with be + past participle. English uses it far more than Spanish, especially in technical and formal writing, because it lets you put the important thing first and leave out who did it.

body.code:
ACTIVE   The mechanic replaced the pump.
PASSIVE  The pump WAS REPLACED (by the mechanic).

Present  The engine IS SERVICED every 500 hours.
Past     The report WAS WRITTEN yesterday.
Perfect  The filter HAS BEEN CHANGED.
Modal    The guard MUST BE REPLACED before use.

body.p: Use it when who did the action is unknown, obvious or irrelevant. Add by only when the agent matters. In a maintenance log, The seals were replaced at 4,300 hours is exactly right: nobody cares which hands did it.

body.code:
WHO    people    The man WHO called you is here.
WHICH  things     The part WHICH broke is expensive.
THAT   both       The tool THAT I need is missing.
WHERE  places     The workshop WHERE I work.
WHOSE  possession The driver WHOSE truck broke down.

body.p: When the relative word is the object of the clause, English lets you drop it entirely — and native speakers usually do: The tool (that) I need is missing. You cannot drop it when it is the subject: The man who called keeps its who.

body.note: Commas change the meaning. The machines that were serviced are working = only those ones. The machines, which were serviced, are working = all of them, and by the way they were serviced.

body.code:
I USED TO drive trucks.          (before, not now)
I DIDN'T USE TO like it.          ← no -d in the negative
DID you USE TO work at night?     ← no -d in the question

body.warn: Do not confuse three similar things: used to + verb = a past habit. be used to + -ing = accustomed (I'm used to working nights). get used to + -ing = becoming accustomed (I'm getting used to it).

body.code:
FIRST — real, possible future
  IF + present simple , ... WILL + verb
  If it rains, we will stop working.

SECOND — imaginary or unlikely present
  IF + past simple , ... WOULD + verb
  If I had more time, I would study every day.

body.p: The if half never takes will or would: If it will rain is wrong. And in the second conditional, the past form does not mean past time — it signals distance from reality. That is why If I were you keeps that old were for every person.

body.note: You can swap the halves; only the comma moves: If it rains, we will stop = We will stop if it rains (no comma when the if comes second).

body.code:
COUNTABLE          UNCOUNTABLE        BOTH
many bolts         much oil           a lot of / lots of
a few bolts        a little oil       some / any
few bolts (≈none)  little oil (≈none) enough
several            a bit of           plenty of

body.p: Watch the difference a single article makes: a few means «some, and that's fine»; few means «almost none, and that's a problem». We have a few filters is reassuring. We have few filters is a warning.

body.code:
SHORT adj    fast → faster → the fastest
LONG adj     expensive → more expensive → the most expensive
IRREGULAR    good/better/best   bad/worse/worst   far/further/furthest

EQUAL        This one is AS powerful AS that one.
NOT EQUAL    It isn't as heavy as the old model.
DOUBLE       THE MORE you service it, THE LONGER it lasts.
CHANGE       It's getting BETTER AND BETTER.

body.p: After a comparative, use than, never that: more powerful than that one. It is a small word, and getting it wrong is very noticeable.

body.code:
FREQUENCY   before the main verb, after BE
  I ALWAYS check the oil.
  He is NEVER late.
  always > usually > often > sometimes > rarely > never

MANNER      normally at the end
  He works CAREFULLY.

TIME        at the end (or the beginning for emphasis)
  I finished the job YESTERDAY.

body.warn: English does not let an adverb sit between the verb and its object: I check the oil carefully ✅, but I check carefully the oil ❌. Spanish allows it, so this mistake survives for years.

body.p: Group them by situation, not alphabetically — that is how you will actually recall them.

list: Machines: break down (fail), start up, shut down, warm up, wear out, run out of.
Problems: sort out (resolve), deal with, look into (investigate), come across (find by chance), end up (finish in a situation).
Work: take on (accept work, hire), carry out (perform), set up (prepare), put off (postpone), call off (cancel), fill in (complete a form).
People: get on with (have a good relationship), take after (resemble a relative), look after (take care of), turn up (arrive), let down (disappoint).

body.key: Every one of these has a formal one-word equivalent, and in speech the phrasal verb is almost always the natural choice. We'll look into it sounds human; We will investigate it sounds like a letter from a lawyer.

body.code:
maintain (v) → maintenance (n) → maintainable (adj)
safe (adj)   → safety (n)      → unsafe → safely (adv)
reliable     → reliability     → unreliable
repair (v/n) → repairable      → irreparable

NOUNS       -tion  -ment  -ity  -ness
ADJECTIVES  -able  -ive   -ous  -ful  -less
OPPOSITES   un-  in-  im-  ir-  dis-

body.p: Learning one word gives you four for free, and it doubles your reading speed: when you meet irreparable for the first time, you don't need a dictionary.

Pick three phrasal verbs a week and force them into real sentences about your own day, not textbook examples. The excavator broke down. We ran out of filters. I'll follow up with the supplier. A phrasal verb you have used out loud five times is yours; one you have only read is not.

chapters.title: Conditionals, reported speech and professional writing
chapters.subtitle: The structures you need to explain causes, report what others said and write an email that gets answered.

body.p: At B2 the goal changes. You are no longer trying to be understood — you are trying to be precise: to say what would have happened, to report a conversation accurately, and to write something a stranger will act on.

body.h: The conditionals as a single system

body.p: Do not learn four separate rules. Learn one idea: how far the situation is from reality, and shift the tense back accordingly.

body.code:
ZERO    general truth        If you heat water, it boils.
FIRST   real future          If it rains, we WILL stop.
SECOND  imaginary present    If I HAD time, I WOULD study.
THIRD   impossible past      If I HAD KNOWN, I WOULD HAVE called.

body.p: Each step back in reality takes one step back in tense. The second conditional uses a past form for a present situation; the third uses the past perfect for a past one. The if half never takes will or would — that is the mistake to watch for.
Real conversation mixes the time frames, and this is where you sound advanced:

body.code:
Past cause → present result:
  If I had studied English at school, I would be working abroad now.

Present cause → past result:
  If I were more careful, I wouldn't have made that mistake.

body.key: The third conditional is the language of diagnosis and accountability: If the filter had been replaced on schedule, the damage would have been avoided. If you write incident reports, this structure is not optional.

body.p: When you report what someone said, you move one step back in time, because the moment of speaking has passed.

body.code:
"I am busy."        → He said he WAS busy.
"I saw it."          → He said he HAD SEEN it.
"I will call you."   → He said he WOULD call me.
"I can fix it."      → He said he COULD fix it.

Also shift:  tomorrow → the next day   ·   here → there
             this → that                ·   now → then

body.note: You do not shift the tense when the statement is still true: He said the engine runs on diesel is fine, because it still does. The shift reflects distance in time, not a mechanical rule.

body.p: Reporting questions is where most people slip. The reported question is no longer a question, so it takes normal word order and no auxiliary:

body.code:
"Where is the manual?"   → He asked where the manual WAS.
                            (not: where was the manual)
"Did you check it?"      → He asked IF I had checked it.

body.p: This is how you express certainty in a diagnosis without claiming more than you know.

list: must be — I'm almost certain it is: It must be the alternator.
might / could be — it's possible: It might be a vacuum leak.
can't be — I'm certain it isn't: It can't be the battery; it's new.

body.p: For the past, add have: The seal must have failed under pressure. The alarm can't have been working.
Some verbs are followed by -ing, others by to. There is no logic to memorise, but there are patterns:

body.code:
+ -ing    enjoy, avoid, finish, keep, suggest, mind, practise, risk
          I avoid working in the rain.

+ to      decide, hope, need, want, manage, offer, refuse, agree
          I managed to fix it.

BOTH, different meaning:
  I stopped smoking.       (I quit)
  I stopped to smoke.      (I paused in order to smoke)
  I remember locking it.   (memory of a past action)
  I remembered to lock it. (I didn't forget)

PRESENT regret   wish + PAST
  I wish I HAD more time.
  If only I SPOKE better English.

PAST regret      wish + PAST PERFECT
  I wish I HAD STUDIED English earlier.

ANNOYANCE        wish + WOULD  (about other people)
  I wish they WOULD STOP making that noise.

body.p: The pattern is the same as the conditionals: one step back in tense equals one step away from reality. If only is simply a stronger, more emotional wish.

body.warn: You cannot use wish + would about yourself: I wish I would study more. For your own behaviour it is I wish I studied more or I should study more.

body.p: Two passive patterns appear constantly in professional English and almost never in courses.

body.code:
IMPERSONAL REPORTING — distance from the claim
  It IS SAID THAT the model is unreliable.
  The pump IS BELIEVED TO HAVE FAILED under load.
  The fault IS THOUGHT TO BE electrical.

CAUSATIVE — you arrange for someone else to do it
  I HAD the engine SERVICED.        (I didn't do it myself)
  We are HAVING the workshop PAINTED.
  I GOT my licence RENEWED.         (more informal)

body.p: The causative is the natural way to talk about work you commissioned. I repaired my truck means you did it; I had my truck repaired means the workshop did. Spanish blurs this; English does not.
When two clauses share a subject, English often compresses the first into a participle. It is one of the clearest markers of a B2+ writer:

body.code:
After I checked the oil, I started the engine.
→ HAVING CHECKED the oil, I started the engine.

Because it was damaged, the filter was replaced.
→ BEING damaged, the filter was replaced.
→ DAMAGED, the filter was replaced.

The report, which was written last week, ...
→ The report, WRITTEN last week, ...

body.warn: The two halves must share the subject. Having checked the oil, the engine started is wrong — it says the engine checked the oil. This is called a dangling participle and it is a classic error in technical reports.

body.h: Articles at B2: the details that give you away

list: No article for general plurals and uncountables: Hydraulic systems require clean oil.
The for something unique or already identified: the relief valve, the manual.
The + adjective for a group: the injured, the unemployed.
No article with institutions used for their purpose: go to work, in hospital (UK), at school.
The with superlatives, ordinals and rivers/seas/mountain ranges; no article with continents, countries and single mountains.

body.code:
ADDING       in addition · furthermore · moreover · what is more
CONTRAST     however · although · despite / in spite of · whereas
RESULT       therefore · consequently · as a result · so
REASON       because · since · as · due to · owing to
EXAMPLE      for instance · such as · in particular
SEQUENCE     first · then · after that · finally

body.warn: Two traps. Although is followed by a clause (Although it was late, we finished); despite / in spite of by a noun or -ing (Despite the delay, Despite being late). And because introduces a clause while because of introduces a noun.

body.h: Collocations: the words that travel together

body.p: At B2 the grammar is rarely the problem — the word combinations are. English fixes which verb goes with which noun, and a wrong pair is understood but sounds foreign.

body.code:
MAKE   a decision · a mistake · progress · an effort · an appointment
DO     the work · a job · research · damage · business
TAKE   responsibility · a break · a risk · measurements · action
MEET   a deadline · a requirement · a standard · demand
RUN    a test · a business · a machine · a check
RAISE  a concern · an issue · awareness
CARRY  out an inspection · out repairs · out a survey

body.key: Make creates something new; do performs an activity. That distinction covers most cases, and the rest you learn by collecting them in pairs, never as single words.

body.code:
INCREASE   rise · go up · grow · climb · double
DECREASE   fall · drop · decline · go down · halve
STABLE     remain steady · level off · plateau
SHARP      significantly · sharply · dramatically
SLIGHT     slightly · marginally · gradually

Failures ROSE SHARPLY in June, then LEVELLED OFF.
Downtime FELL BY 20%.  (by = the difference)
Downtime FELL TO 20 hours.  (to = the final figure)

body.note: by and to are not interchangeable and the difference is money: costs fell by 30% means they dropped a third; costs fell to 30% means they are now less than a third of what they were.

body.h: On the phone and in meetings

list: Opening: This is Luis calling about the pump order. / I'm calling to follow up on…
Not understanding: Sorry, could you repeat that? / Could you speak a bit more slowly, please? / Just to make sure I understood — you mean…?
Buying time: Let me check and get back to you. / That's a good question — give me a moment.
Interrupting politely: Sorry to interrupt, but… / Can I just add something here?
Disagreeing: I see your point, but… / I'm not sure I agree — in my experience…
Closing: So, to summarise… / I'll send you an email confirming that.

body.key: «Sorry, could you repeat that?» is the most valuable sentence at B2. Pretending to understand is what actually breaks a conversation — asking never does.

body.p: Professional English is shorter than most learners expect. One idea per paragraph, the request in the first three lines, no decoration.

body.quote:
Dear Mr. Ramírez,

I am writing to request a quotation for a hydraulic pump seal kit for a CAT 320D.

Could you please confirm availability and estimated delivery time? We would need the parts before 15 September.

I look forward to hearing from you.

Kind regards,
Luis Blandón

list: I am writing to… — states the purpose immediately
Could you please… — polite request; more formal than can you
I would be grateful if you could… — one step more formal
Please find attached… — for documents
I look forward to hearing from you — standard closing (remember: hearing, not hear)

body.warn: Match the opening and the closing. Dear Sir/Madam → Yours faithfully when you don't know the name; Dear Mr. Smith → Yours sincerely when you do. Kind regards is safe for almost everything and is what most people actually use.

body.key: Read your email once and delete every sentence that does not either give information or ask for something. English business writing rewards brevity in a way Spanish correspondence does not.

chapters.title: Register: sounding like a professional
chapters.subtitle: Inversion, cleft sentences, hedging and the difference between correct English and convincing English.

body.p: At C1 grammar is no longer the obstacle. The question becomes: does your English sound like the person you are? The tools in this chapter are about emphasis, distance and precision — how to stress a point, how to be careful with a claim, how to choose the register the situation calls for.
When a negative or limiting adverbial opens the sentence, the subject and the auxiliary swap places, as in a question:

body.code:
Never have I seen such a badly maintained machine.
Not only did they ignore the alarm, but they also kept working.
Rarely does a failure happen without warning.
Not until the engine had cooled down did we open the radiator.
Under no circumstances should the guard be removed.

body.p: Note that in the last example the inversion happens in the main clause, not inside the opening phrase. This is the detail most learners get wrong.

body.warn: Inversion is formal and emphatic. Used once in a report it lands; used three times it sounds theatrical. Reserve it for the sentence that matters most.

body.p: A cleft splits one sentence in two to put a single element under the light. It is how you correct, contrast or emphasise without raising your voice:

body.code:
Neutral:  The seal failed, not the pump.
It-cleft:  It was the seal that failed, not the pump.
What-cleft: What caused the failure was contaminated oil.
All-cleft:  All I need is a torque wrench.
The reason: The reason we stopped was a safety concern.

body.key: Clefts are the most useful advanced structure for meetings. When someone misattributes a problem, «What actually happened was…» corrects the record firmly and without confrontation.

body.p: Beginners state facts. Professionals state facts with a stated degree of confidence, because overclaiming destroys credibility the first time you are wrong.

body.code:
Blunt:   The contamination caused the failure.
Hedged:  The failure APPEARS TO HAVE BEEN caused by contamination.
         The evidence POINTS TO a seal failure.
         This WOULD SUGGEST a problem with the relief valve.
         There is A STRONG LIKELIHOOD that the filter was bypassed.
         The damage is, IN ALL PROBABILITY, cumulative.

body.p: Hedging is not weakness or vagueness — it is precision about how much you know. The opposite skill matters too: when you are certain, say so plainly, and the contrast makes it count.

body.h: The subjunctive after demands and recommendations

body.p: After verbs and adjectives of requirement, English uses the bare infinitive — no -s, no tense agreement. It sounds strange until you notice it everywhere in manuals and regulations:

body.code:
The manual recommends that the filter BE REPLACED every 500 hours.
They insisted that he ATTEND the safety briefing.
It is essential that everyone WEAR a helmet.
We propose that the schedule BE REVIEWED.

body.h: Nominalisation: the texture of formal writing

body.p: Formal written English turns verbs into nouns. It makes the prose compact and impersonal — useful in reports, poisonous in excess.

body.code:
They inspected the machine and it failed.
→ The inspection revealed a failure.

We decided to replace it because it was worn.
→ The decision to replace it was based on wear.

The pump was not maintained, so it broke.
→ The breakdown resulted from inadequate maintenance.

body.note: Notice what nominalisation removes: the person responsible. That is exactly why it dominates official writing — and exactly why you should use it consciously, not by default.

body.code:
INFORMAL   The engine packed up.
NEUTRAL    The engine broke down.
FORMAL     The engine suffered a catastrophic failure.

ask for → request        ·   put off → postpone
find out → ascertain     ·   get rid of → eliminate
look into → investigate  ·   carry out → conduct

body.p: See the pattern: the informal half of each pair is almost always the phrasal verb, and the formal half is a single Latin-derived word — often close to Spanish. That is an advantage for you: your instinct for the formal word is usually right. The harder skill is the opposite — knowing when the phrasal verb is the better choice, because it sounds natural rather than stiff.

list: boil down to — reduce to the essential point: It all boils down to poor maintenance.
account for — explain, or represent a proportion: Wear accounts for 60% of failures.
rule out — eliminate a possibility: We ruled out an electrical fault.
iron out — resolve remaining small problems: We ironed out the last issues.
gloss over — avoid dealing with something properly: The report glossed over the safety failures.
weigh up — consider carefully: We weighed up the options.
phase out — withdraw gradually: They are phasing out that model.

body.code:
ADDING       moreover, furthermore, what is more
CONTRASTING  however, nevertheless, that said, whereas
CAUSE        consequently, hence, as a result, thereby
CONCEDING    admittedly, granted, even so, to be fair
CONCLUDING   overall, on balance, all things considered

body.p: These are the signposts that let a reader follow an argument without effort. That said and admittedly are particularly valuable: they show you have considered the counter-argument, which makes the rest of your case more credible.
Inversion is the loud tool. English has quieter ones you will use far more often.

body.code:
EMPHATIC DO       We DID check the pressure.  (contradicting)
                  It DOES seem unusual.

FRONTING          That valve, I replaced last week.
                  Serious, the damage was not.  (rare, literary)

REFLEXIVE         The manual itself says otherwise.

ADVERBS           This is precisely the problem.
                  The fault lies squarely with maintenance.

body.p: Emphatic do is especially useful in disagreement, because it concedes and corrects at once: We did follow the procedure — the failure happened anyway.
Advanced English removes what the listener can reconstruct. Repeating it in full is grammatically correct and sounds heavy.

body.code:
— Have you checked the pressure?
— I have.                    (not: I have checked the pressure)

— Will it need a new seal?
— It might DO.  /  I think SO.  /  I hope NOT.

He replaced the filter and (he) tested the machine.
The first option is cheaper than the second (one).

body.note: so and not stand in for a whole clause: I think so, I'm afraid not, If so, we'll postpone it. Using them is one of the cheapest ways to sound fluent.

body.p: Formal English packs information into the noun phrase rather than into extra sentences. Reading it is a C1 skill; writing it is a choice.

body.code:
The recently identified hydraulic fluid contamination issue
 │       │          │         │        │            │
 det  adverb    participle  modifiers        head noun

A delay in the delivery of the replacement parts ordered last month

body.warn: This construction is why technical documents are hard to read. Use it to be compact, not to be impressive: if a reader has to go back to the start of the phrase, split the sentence in two.

body.p: You already know how to soften a claim. The complementary skill is knowing how to strengthen one — and how to alternate, because a text that only hedges sounds evasive.

body.code:
SOFTEN   appears to · would suggest · in all probability · tends to
         it may be that · to some extent · arguably

STRENGTHEN clearly · undoubtedly · there is no question that
           the evidence is conclusive · invariably · demonstrably

body.key: The rhetorical effect comes from the contrast. Hedge the uncertain parts carefully, then state the one thing you are sure of without any hedge at all — that sentence will carry the whole document.

body.code:
thin / slim / skinny        neutral · positive · negative
cheap / inexpensive         negative quality · neutral
stubborn / determined       negative · positive
interfere / intervene       unwelcome · legitimate
aggressive / assertive      hostile · confident
noticed / spotted / detected  neutral · alert · technical

body.p: A dictionary will give you all six as translations of the same Spanish word. Choosing the wrong one does not produce an error a teacher would mark — it produces an impression you did not intend, which is worse.

body.h: Idioms that appear in professional English

list: a bottleneck — the point that limits everything else
a workaround — a temporary solution that avoids the real problem
a stopgap — a short-term fix
the root cause — the underlying cause, as opposed to the symptom
downtime — time a machine or system is out of service
a backlog — accumulated pending work
to cut corners — to do something badly to save time or money
to be on the same page — to share the same understanding
to touch base — to make brief contact
to escalate — to pass an issue to a higher level

body.note: Use idioms sparingly in writing and freely in speech. A report full of idioms reads as unserious; a conversation without any reads as translated.

body.h: The structure of a technical report

body.code:
1. SUMMARY        the conclusion, in three lines, first
2. BACKGROUND     what was observed and when
3. FINDINGS       the evidence, separated from interpretation
4. ANALYSIS       what the evidence means, hedged appropriately
5. RECOMMENDATIONS  numbered, actionable, with an owner

body.p: English professional writing is conclusion first. Spanish tradition often builds the argument and reveals the conclusion at the end; in English that reads as burying the point. Say what you found, then explain how.

body.key: Separate findings from analysis ruthlessly. «The oil sample showed 45 ppm of silicon» is a finding. «This indicates air filter bypass» is analysis. Mixing them is what makes a report impossible to challenge — and therefore impossible to trust.

list: Signposting: I'll cover three points today. / Let me turn to the second issue. / Coming back to what I mentioned earlier…
Handling questions: That's outside the scope of this report, but my understanding is… / I'd rather not speculate — let me confirm and come back to you.
Proposing: What if we…? / Would you be open to…? / One option would be to…
Conceding ground: That's a fair point. / I take your point on cost, though I'd still argue…
Holding your position: I understand the constraint, but I can't recommend that on safety grounds.

body.p: Notice how much of C1 is not vocabulary but stance: conceding, qualifying, refusing without hostility. That is the register that makes a non-native speaker sound senior rather than merely correct.

body.quote: The failure appears to have originated in the hydraulic circuit rather than the pump itself. Analysis of the oil sample revealed a high silicon content, which points to contamination through a damaged air filter. Had the filter been replaced at the scheduled interval, the damage would in all probability have been avoided. Admittedly, the service records are incomplete. We therefore recommend that the maintenance schedule be reviewed.

body.key: Five sentences containing hedging, nominalisation, an inverted third conditional (Had the filter been replaced…), a concession and the subjunctive. Nothing exotic — this is simply how a competent technical report reads in English.

chapters.title: Writing that gets read
chapters.subtitle: Participle clauses, impersonal reporting, cause-and-effect vocabulary and the structure of an email people actually answer.

body.p: At C1 the grammar is mostly behind you. What separates a good report from a bad one is structure and precision: saying exactly how strong your claim is, and putting the important part where the reader will actually see it.
Participle clauses compress a sentence without losing meaning — the backbone of technical writing.

body.code:
Having checked the pressure, we replaced the valve.   (after)
Working under load, the pump overheats.               (while)
Damaged by vibration, the bracket failed.             (passive)

body.warn: The hidden subject must match the main clause. Having replaced the seal, the machine worked says the machine replaced its own seal. That is a dangling participle, and in a report it reads as carelessness.

body.p: Investigations rarely want to name a person. English has a ready-made structure for that:

body.code:
It is believed that the seal failed.
The seal is believed to have failed.
The delay is thought to have been caused by a parts shortage.

body.p: Past reference takes the perfect infinitive: is believed to have failed. The same pattern works with is said to, is expected to, is reported to.

body.h: Cause and effect, in both directions

body.p: Half the mistakes in technical English are a reversed causal chain. Keep the two families apart:

list: Cause → effect: led to · resulted in · brought about · gave rise to · triggered
Effect → cause: resulted from · stemmed from · was attributable to · arose from
Partial cause: contributed to · was a factor in · compounded

body.key: result in = cause. result from = be caused by. One preposition turns your sentence around, and nobody will tell you.

body.h: The comma that changes the fleet

body.code:
The pumps that failed were replaced.     → only those ones
The pumps, which failed, were replaced.  → all of them failed

body.p: Defining clauses take no comma (that or which); non-defining ones take commas and only which. This is not decoration: it decides whether you replaced two pumps or twenty.
Vague quantities make a report sound unreliable. English is rich here, so use it:

body.code:
small    a slight / marginal increase · edged up · tailed off
large    a sharp / steep rise · soared · plummeted
steady   a gradual decline · levelled off · plateaued
about    roughly · in the region of · just under · upwards of

body.p: Downtime edged up in March, then plateaued at just under 40 hours. Three precise words carry more authority than a paragraph of hedging.
In writing you have no tone of voice. English puts stress with structure instead:

body.code:
What surprised us was the cost, not the delay.
What we need is a second pump.
The vibration did stop after the alignment.
It was only after the third test that the fault appeared.

body.note: One per paragraph. Used twice in a row, emphasis stops being emphasis.

body.p: Three moves, always in this order: an apologetic opener, a distancing verb, and — this is the one people forget — an alternative.

body.code:
Direct:      We can't deliver on Friday.
Professional: Unfortunately, we won't be able to deliver on Friday.
Diplomatic:  I'm afraid Friday is looking unlikely — would Monday work?

steps: Purpose — I'm writing to confirm the delivery date for the hydraulic kit.
Context — As discussed on Tuesday, the original date was 12 March.
Request — Could you confirm whether the revised date works on your side?
Close — Happy to call if that's easier. Best regards, …

body.p: One idea per paragraph and the request on its own line. Most people read the first two lines and the last one — so never bury the ask at the bottom.

body.key: Verbs that make you sound like you know what you are doing: establish · ascertain · corroborate · preclude · mitigate · warrant · defer · escalate. The evidence did not corroborate the operator's account, but the wear pattern warrants a full inspection.
